subjects.displayTitle: Personal instructions: wisdom addressed to a life
subjects.introduction: Greet your household with a loving face when the sun rises; rest, because a body worn out by hardship can serve no one; consult with your husband before deciding about Africa; write often, whether or not a reply comes. Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá addressed counsel of this kind to particular people in particular straits, and in it a whole spiritual life descends into the texture of a single day: a child’s schooling, a debt, a difficult colleague, a letter that must reach the right hands. Is this an absolute command or wisdom offered in goodwill, and whose circumstances does it fit? Confucius gave opposite answers to two disciples who asked the same question, knowing one needed urging and the other restraint [1]; Paul, pleading for Onesimus, hoped for a kindness freely given rather than exacted [2]. The journey leads on into wisdom as the measure of every act, into permission to visit, and into business and property matters, where trust in God meets practical skill. Beneath every instruction runs a remembrance: the one counselled is seen in the light of what they may become.

questions: How does the opening instruction to greet one’s household with kindness change your understanding of spiritual guidance? Which practical requests for care give that principle unexpected depth?

Compare the passage distinguishing counsel from an absolute command with the directions to consult, act freely or observe an explicit law. What questions about recipient, authority and circumstances help you read each responsibly?

In Analects 11.22, different disciples receive different counsel. How do the instructions here to travel, remain, study or rest illuminate the relation between a shared purpose and a particular person’s needs?

What do the passages about employment, contracts, learning and caring for family suggest about the relation between trust in God and practical means? How might the connected subjects of wisdom and business, financial and property matters deepen this inquiry?

Read Philemon alongside the requests for assistance and reconciliation in this collection. How do affection, obligation, freedom and fairness shape a response to another person, and where do the texts’ different settings matter most?

What does it mean to be remembered when a reply is delayed or a meeting is impossible? Return to the closing passages on nearness and becoming: how might receiving encouragement call forth something that is not yet fully realized in a life?

references.label: 1 · Analects 11.22 · Different counsel, attentive teaching
references.note: Read Analects 11.22 in James Legge’s translation. Two disciples ask about putting a teaching into practice immediately, and Confucius gives different answers. When questioned about this, he explains that one needs encouragement while the other needs restraint. Compare this with the instructions here to travel, remain, study, rest or consult. What must a teacher understand about a person before offering helpful counsel? The Analects presents a Confucian account of moral formation; these Baha’i texts have their own religious authority and circumstances. The comparison invites attention to the recipient without assuming that every difference in advice has the same explanation.

references.label: 2 · Philemon 1:8–21 · Appeal, affection and willing action
references.note: Read Philemon 1:8–21 in the King James Version. Paul appeals on behalf of Onesimus, asks that he be received as a beloved brother, offers to assume what is owed, and wishes the benefit to be freely given. Read this within its early Christian setting and the reality of enslavement that the letter addresses. Compare its appeal through affection with the compilation’s distinction between counsel and an absolute command, and with requests for practical help. What makes a response willing, and how can love change an existing relationship? Paul’s apostolic relationship and the authority of the Baha’i passages remain distinct; consider both the affinities and the limits of the comparison.
